hints: For one pair of cities, list the flights needed so that someone in either city can go out in the morning and come back in the evening.
Count the ordered pairs of cities, then the flights each needs.
1.why:
To go from X to Y and come back the same day, you need a morning flight X→Y and an evening flight Y→X. Every direct link between two cities that people use therefore needs 4 flights: morning both ways and evening both ways.

Each of the 45 pairs needs 4 flights: 45 × 4 = 180. (45 or 90 forgets the return trip or one of the two directions.)

hints: For one pair of cities, list the flights needed so that someone in either city can go out in the morning and come back in the evening.
Every flight touches a hub. Count each hub's links to the other 9 cities, but don't count a hub-to-hub link twice.
2.why:
To go from X to Y and come back the same day, you need a morning flight X→Y and an evening flight Y→X. Every direct link between two cities that people use therefore needs 4 flights: morning both ways and evening both ways.

Each hub links to 9 cities: 3 × 9 = 27 links, minus the 3 hub-to-hub links counted twice = 24 links. 24 × 4 = 96. Any two non-hub cities connect through one hub.

hints: For one pair of cities, list the flights needed so that someone in either city can go out in the morning and come back in the evening.
Each outer city can only fly to one G1 city. Count the links, then multiply by the flights each link needs.
3.why:
To go from X to Y and come back the same day, you need a morning flight X→Y and an evening flight Y→X. Every direct link between two cities that people use therefore needs 4 flights: morning both ways and evening both ways.

Allowed links: A–G2 (3), B–G3 (2), C–G4 (2) and the G1 links A–B, B–C, C–A. The 7 outer cities each hang off one G1 city, so all 7 of those links are needed.

The official answer counts all 3 G1 links: 10 links × 4 = 40. Note: if a B-to-C trip may change planes at A, only 2 G1 links are needed and the count would be 36. The key treats every G1 pair as a direct link, so go with 40 here.

hints: For one pair of cities, list the flights needed so that someone in either city can go out in the morning and come back in the evening.
After the change, A links only to B, and C–A is gone. Count the links before and after.
4.why:
To go from X to Y and come back the same day, you need a morning flight X→Y and an evening flight Y→X. Every direct link between two cities that people use therefore needs 4 flights: morning both ways and evening both ways.

Allowed links: A–G2 (3), B–G3 (2), C–G4 (2) and the G1 links A–B, B–C, C–A. The 7 outer cities each hang off one G1 city, so all 7 of those links are needed.

The official answer counts all 3 G1 links: 10 links × 4 = 40. Note: if a B-to-C trip may change planes at A, only 2 G1 links are needed and the count would be 36. The key treats every G1 pair as a direct link, so go with 40 here.

After the change: A–B and B–C, plus the 7 outer cities (G2 moves under B or C). That's 9 links, 36 flights. The reduction is 40 − 36 = 4.

hints: Write the time for each route as a formula in the number of cars on it. Then try each split of the 4 cars.
A split works only if no single car can switch routes and arrive sooner.
5.why:
Route A-M-B with k cars takes 6 + 3(k−1) + 20 + 0.9(k−1) = 26 + 3.9(k−1). Route A-N-B with j cars takes 20 + (j−1) + 6 + 3(j−1) = 26 + 4(j−1).

Split 2 and 2: A-M-B takes 29.9 and A-N-B takes 30. A car that switches joins a route with 3 cars (33.8 or 34), so nobody gains. A 3–1 split fails: a car on the 3-car route saves time by moving.

So 2 cars take A-N-B.

hints: Let a, b, c be the cars on A-M-B, A-N-B and A-M-N-B. The A-M road carries a + c cars; the N-B road carries b + c.
Try the splits where no route has all 4 cars. In the right one every car takes the same time.
7.why:
With a cars on A-M-B, b on A-N-B and c on A-M-N-B: A-M takes 6 + 3(a+c−1), N-B takes 6 + 3(b+c−1), M-N takes 7 + (c−1), M-B takes 20 + 0.9(a−1), A-N takes 20 + (b−1).

a = 1, b = 1, c = 2: A-M = 12, M-B = 20, A-N = 20, N-B = 12, M-N = 8. Every route takes 32 minutes. Check any one car moving: each move puts it on a slower route, so this is the only split that holds.

2 cars take A-M-N-B.

8.why:

a = 1, b = 1, c = 2: A-M = 12, M-B = 20, A-N = 20, N-B = 12, M-N = 8. Every route takes 32 minutes. Check any one car moving: each move puts it on a slower route, so this is the only split that holds.

The time is 32 minutes. 29.9 and 30 were the times before the new road, and that split no longer holds.

hints: Let x be the number in only P (= only C = only M) and y the number in all three. What does 200 give you?
Write each "below 80th percentile" count in terms of x and the pair groups, then use the ratio 4:2:1.
9.why:
Let x be the count at or above 80 in only P (also only C, only M) and y the count in all three. 3x + 150 + y = 200, so 3x + y = 50.

Below 80 in P = 2x + (C and M only), in C = 2x + (P and M only), in M = 2x + (P and C only). With the ratio 4k : 2k : k and the three pair groups adding to 150: 6x + 150 = 7k. With x at most 16, x = 3 (k = 24) or x = 10 (k = 30).

x = 3: PC 18, PM 42, CM 90, all three 41. x = 10: PC 10, PM 40, CM 80, all three 20.

The separate test is for those at or above 80 in P but not eligible for the AET, which means only P: x = 3 or 10.

hints: How many projects does each employee work on, and how many points does each kind give per person?
A challenging team has 5 people, a standard one has 4.
31.why:
Each person works in one team every month, so 5 projects. A challenging project gives 200/5 = 40 points each, a standard one 100/4 = 25. With k challenging projects: 125 + 15k, so the possible totals are 125, 140, 155, 170, 185 and 200.

150 is not on the list.

hints: 185 = 125 + 15k. How many challenging projects did Aneek work on?
If Aneek missed T2's challenging month, where could Aneek be in month 2, and can Aneek reach T3 in month 3 from there?
32.why:
Each person works in one team every month, so 5 projects. A challenging project gives 200/5 = 40 points each, a standard one 100/4 = 25. With k challenging projects: 125 + 15k, so the possible totals are 125, 140, 155, 170, 185 and 200.

185 means 4 challenging projects: Aneek was in Ti in month i for four months. Option D skips T2 in month 2.

Aneek is in T1 in month 1. Not going to T2 means Aneek is in T1 or T5 in month 2. Between months 2 and 3, T1 and T5 only swap people with each other, and T3 only takes people from T2. So Aneek can't be in T3 in month 3. D can't be true.
